# Can I Change All Tires to Use Different Sidewall Ratio?

You are asking whether an AWD Volvo V60 CC can safely transition from 235/50R18 to 235/60R18 tires, provided you install the new sidewall height on all four wheels simultaneously. While mixing different ratios on a single axle is universally prohibited due to drivetrain stress, changing all four tires at once introduces a distinct set of dynamics that requires careful analysis beyond simple compatibility checks.

The most critical factor in your decision is not just the static dimensions, but how the change affects the final drive ratio and ABS/ESP calibration. When you increase the sidewall height from 50 to 60 while keeping the width constant, the overall tire diameter increases. Mathematically, the difference in section height is 10% of the width (50 vs 60), which translates to a roughly 5% increase in overall diameter depending on the aspect ratio calculation specifics relative to the rim diameter.

Most modern vehicles, including your Volvo V60, rely on wheel speed sensors to calculate vehicle speed via the ABS and ESC modules. These systems expect the tires to rotate at a specific circumference defined by the manufacturer's original equipment (OE) specifications. Increasing the tire diameter means the wheels rotate fewer times per mile than the ECU anticipates. If the speed sensor reads 100 km/h based on rotation count, but the larger tires are physically covering more ground per rotation, the vehicle is actually traveling faster than indicated. This creates a discrepancy where your dashboard speedometer under-reads the true speed.

While this discrepancy might seem minor in a standard two-wheel-drive car, it becomes a significant liability in an All-Wheel Drive system. The AWD logic in the V60 depends on precise synchronization between the front and rear axles. If the effective gear ratio changes significantly due to larger tires, the Torsen center differential or electronic torque vectoring system may interpret normal driving conditions as slip events. This can lead to unnecessary engagement of the clutch pack, reduced fuel efficiency, and potentially erratic behavior in the traction control algorithms.

Furthermore, there is a practical implementation hurdle regarding tire pressure monitoring systems (TPMS). The new 235/60R18 tires will have a different volume and air spring characteristics compared to the original setup. While you can relearn the TPMS sensors after mounting the new tires, the underlying physical change in diameter remains.

If your primary motivation for the upgrade is ground clearance or ride comfort, you must weigh these benefits against the potential for drivetrain strain and calibration issues. In many high-performance AWD platforms, manufacturers explicitly warn against changing the tire size unless it falls within a very narrow tolerance band (usually +/- 3mm in overall diameter).

A safer alternative often overlooked is to search for tires that match your current 235/50R18 dimensions but offer improved wear characteristics or noise cancellation. If you must change the profile, consult a professional tire technician who can verify if the specific brand and model you are considering has been cleared by Volvo for use in V60 AWD models, as some manufacturers provide specific fitment data that overrides general calculations.

Ultimately, while installing identical tires with a larger sidewall on all four corners avoids the immediate mechanical incompatibility of mixed ratios, it alters the vehicle's fundamental gearing and sensor calibration. Proceed with caution, and ensure you understand the long-term implications for your AWD system's performance and safety features before making the switch.
